sections.text: Lenders work backward from your income: they take a share of gross monthly income, subtract your existing debt payments, set aside room for taxes and insurance, and turn what is left into a maximum loan. For a household earning $84,000 a year with $600 a month in other debts and $45,000 for a down payment, at an assumed 6.5% rate on a 30-year loan, a 36% debt ratio gives a maximum price of about $288,012. At 28% it is $217,133. The ratio you pick moves the answer by tens of thousands of dollars, so it is worth understanding what it means.

The 28/36 rule is a traditional lending rule of thumb with two tests. The front-end ratio says housing costs (principal, interest, taxes and insurance, called PITI) should not exceed 28% of gross monthly income. The back-end ratio says all monthly debt payments, housing included, should not exceed 36%. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau defines the debt-to-income ratio as monthly debt payments divided by gross monthly income and notes that different loan products and lenders set different limits. So treat 28/36 as a conservative guideline, not a legal threshold, and ask your lender which limits apply to your loan.

Here the monthly gross income is $7,000. The front-end test allows 28% of that, or $1,960, for housing. The back-end test allows 36% of $7,000, which is $2,520, minus $600 of other debts, or $1,920 for housing. The lower of the two controls, so the back-end test binds at $1,920 a month.
How the calculator converts that payment into a price

items: Maximum total debt = monthly income x chosen ratio.
Housing budget = maximum total debt - existing monthly debts.
The calculator reserves 20% of the housing budget for taxes and insurance, and the other 80% is the principal and interest payment.
The maximum loan is the amount that payment would repay over the term at the entered rate.
Maximum price = maximum loan + down payment.

sections.text: Note that the House Affordability Calculator applies whichever percentage you choose as the total debt ratio, not as a separate front-end cap. That is why its 28% setting is stricter than the classic rule.

The 43% row shows what a higher setting does. Some loan programs allow ratios that high, but approval at that level leaves little room for repairs, savings or a pay cut. The bank's maximum is not a recommendation.

Each $100 of monthly debt removes about $12,657 from the price in this case, so clearing a $300 car payment adds roughly $37,971 of buying power. That often beats saving for a larger down payment. A one-point change in the rate moves the price by roughly $23,000 to $28,000 here, which is why a real quote matters more than a headline rate.

At the 36% price, the 20% reserve is $384 a month. That equals 1.6% of the price a year, for example property tax of 1.2% and insurance of 0.4%. Those percentages are assumptions; tax rates and insurance premiums vary widely by location, so replace them with the real figures for homes you are considering. The calculator does not add mortgage insurance. With $45,000 down on $288,012 you are at 15.6%, below 20%, so a conventional loan usually brings mortgage insurance. At an assumed 0.7% of the loan per year that is about $141.76 a month, which would come out of the same housing budget and reduce the loan you can carry. The CFPB explains that you can request cancellation when the balance is scheduled to fall to 80% of the original home value, and lenders must end it automatically at 78% if you are current.

items: Treating the maximum as the target. Choose the price that leaves room for savings, repairs and income changes, then confirm it with your own monthly budget.
Leaving out non-mortgage housing costs: utilities, maintenance, condo or association fees. They are not in PITI.
Counting only the down payment as cash needed. Closing costs and moving expenses come on top.
Using the starting rate for a loan whose rate can change. For an adjustable loan, test the payment at a higher rate.
Comparing gross ratios with take-home pay. A 36% share of gross income is a larger share of what lands in your account.

sections.text: When these numbers do not apply

The calculation uses fixed assumptions: a fixed rate, a flat 20% tax and insurance reserve, and no mortgage insurance. It ignores credit score, which affects rates, and lender rules about reserves and employment. It also assumes your listed debts are accurate. Treat the result as a planning range, then get pre-approval for a real limit. Enter your own income, debts, down payment and quoted rate into the House Affordability Calculator.

sections.heading: Find Your Number
sections.body: Ready to get your personalized maximum home price? The House Affordability Calculator walks through the same math lenders use, including DTI limits, PMI estimates, and your specific max home price.
